sources: Briggs, Katernine M. An Encyclopedia of Fairies: Hobgoblins, Brownies, Bogies, and Other Supernatural Creatures. New York: Pantheon Books, 1976, 375–376.
Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: Solitary fairies are one of the two kinds of fairy in Irish and Scottish folklore. The other kind is the trooping fairy. Trooping fairies spent their time with others of their own kind, dancing and making merry. Solitary fairies preferred their own company to that of others. They were often ill-natured. The most famous of the kind was the leprechaun, said to be a fairy shoemaker who hid his wealth. The leprechaun kept his store of gold away from all. The cluricaune of the old tales was another figure of the solitary sort. The leprechaun made shoes in his own work, and the cluricaune kept watch near the drink of the house. Both figures stayed apart from the troop. The one who met them leaned in the earth the common caution that the lone fairy gave no help and asked for none from any traveler who crossed its way.
